points.description: Sets up the structure: tracks counts of values (a value's count only increases; the m-th person's number is 1 + count among first m-2, so each new term is determined by the previous term's count). Shows that large values keep being forced, e.g. every value that appears does so with controlled frequency, and that every value chosen after the first N people has count related to earlier appearances (a value k>1 can only appear after k-1 appeared, etc.).

levels.says: Some correct basic observations about counts/recurrence but not developed into a usable lemma.

points.description: Proves that only finitely many integers appear infinitely many times in the combined sequences (equivalently, the set of values appearing infinitely often is bounded / finite, with a rigorous argument).

levels.says: Correct claim with an incomplete or partly flawed argument.

points.description: Uses finiteness of the infinitely-recurring values to show that eventually the sequence is determined by a finite-state/bounded-count behaviour: after some point, every term is one of the finitely many recurring values, and the pattern of which values go to which parity (boys vs girls) is controlled.

levels.says: Partial progress, e.g. reduces to eventual bounded values but does not control the parity/position structure.

points.description: Completes the argument that the boys' sequence or the girls' sequence is eventually periodic (rigorous combination, e.g. pigeonhole on states / dependence of terms on the previous term's count), concluding (i) or (ii).

levels.says: Right conclusion with a gap in the periodicity argument.

rubric.notes: Full marks need a rigorous proof that only finitely many values recur infinitely often and a complete deduction of eventual periodicity for boys or girls. Partial credit for correct lemmas or observations not rigorously combined. Equivalent wording and alternative valid approaches earn marks.
